{{Short description|Algebraic stack in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''moduli stack of elliptic curves''', denoted as <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math> or <math>\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}</math>, is an [[algebraic stack]] over <math>\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})</math> classifying [[elliptic curves]]. Note that it is a special case of the [[moduli stack of algebraic curves]] <math>\mathcal{M}_{g,n}</math>. In particular its points with values in some field correspond to elliptic curves over the field, and more generally morphisms from a scheme <math>S</math> to it correspond to elliptic curves over <math>S</math>. The construction of this space spans over a century because of the various generalizations of elliptic curves as the field has developed. All of these generalizations are contained in <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math>.

== Properties ==

=== Smooth Deligne-Mumford stack ===
The moduli stack of elliptic curves is a smooth separated [[Deligne–Mumford stack]] of finite type over <math>\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})</math>, but is not a scheme as elliptic curves have non-trivial automorphisms.

=== j-invariant ===
There is a [[proper morphism]] of <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math> to the [[Affine space|affine line]], the coarse moduli space of elliptic curves, given by the [[J-invariant|''j''-invariant]] of an elliptic curve.

== Construction over the complex numbers ==
It is a classical observation that every elliptic curve over <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is classified by its [[Period matrix|periods]]. Given a basis for its integral homology <math>\alpha,\beta \in H_1(E,\mathbb{Z})</math> and a global holomorphic [[differential form]] <math>\omega \in \Gamma(E,\Omega^1_E)</math> (which exists since it is smooth and the dimension of the space of such differentials is equal to the [[Arithmetic genus|genus]], 1), the integrals<math display="block">\begin{bmatrix}\int_\alpha \omega & \int_\beta\omega \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\omega_1 & \omega_2 \end{bmatrix}</math>give the generators for a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-lattice of rank 2 inside of <math>\mathbb{C}</math><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Silverman, Joseph H. |author-link=Joseph H. Silverman |title=The arithmetic of elliptic curves |date=2009 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=978-0-387-09494-6 |edition=2nd |location=New York |oclc=405546184}}</ref> <sup>pg 158</sup>. Conversely, given an integral lattice <math>\Lambda</math> of rank <math>2</math> inside of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, there is an embedding of the [[complex torus]] <math>E_\Lambda = \mathbb{C}/\Lambda</math> into <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math> from the [[Weierstrass P function]]<ref name=":0" /> <sup>pg 165</sup>. This isomorphic correspondence <math>\phi:\mathbb{C}/\Lambda \to E(\mathbb{C})</math> is given by<math display="block">z \mapsto [\wp(z,\Lambda),\wp'(z,\Lambda),1] \in \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})</math>and holds up to [[Homothetic transformation|homothety]] of the lattice <math>\Lambda</math>, which is the [[equivalence relation]]<math display="block">z\Lambda \sim \Lambda ~\text{for}~ z \in \mathbb{C} \setminus\{0\}</math>It is standard to then write the lattice in the form <math>\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\cdot \tau</math> for <math>\tau \in \mathfrak{h}</math>, an element of the [[upper half-plane]], since the lattice <math>\Lambda</math> could be multiplied by <math>\omega_1^{-1}</math>, and <math>\tau,-\tau</math> both generate the same sublattice. Then, the upper half-plane gives a [[parameter space]] of all elliptic curves over <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. There is an additional equivalence of curves given by the action of the<math display="block">\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})= \left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix} \in \text{Mat}_{2,2}(\mathbb{Z}) : ad-bc = 1 
\right\}</math>where an elliptic curve defined by the lattice <math>\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\cdot \tau</math> is isomorphic to curves defined by the lattice <math>\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\cdot \tau'</math> given by the [[Möbius transformation|modular action]]<math display="block"> \begin{align}
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix} \cdot \tau &= \frac{a\tau + b}{c\tau + d} \\
&= \tau'
\end{align}</math>Then, the moduli stack of elliptic curves over <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is given by the stack quotient<math display="block"> \mathcal{M}_{1,1} \cong[\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\backslash\mathfrak{h}]</math>Note some authors construct this moduli space by instead using the action of the [[Modular group]] <math>\text{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) = \text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})/\{\pm I\}</math>. In this case, the points in <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math> having only trivial stabilizers are dense.

[[File:The_modular_group_PSL_2(Z).svg|thumb|500px|Fundamental domains of the action of <math>\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math> on the upper half-plane are shown here as pairs of ideal triangles of different colors sharing an edge.  The "standard" fundamental domain is shown with darker edges. Suitably identifying points on the boundary of this region, we obtain the coarse moduli space of elliptic curves.  The stacky points at <math>\tau = i</math> and <math>\tau = e^{2\pi i / 3}, e^{\pi i / 3}</math> are on the boundary of this region.]]

<math> \qquad </math>

=== Stacky/Orbifold points ===
Generically, the points in <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math> are isomorphic to the classifying stack <math>B(\mathbb{Z}/2)</math> since every elliptic curve corresponds to a double cover of <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>, so the <math>\mathbb{Z}/2</math>-action on the point corresponds to the involution of these two branches of the covering. There are a few special points<ref name=":2">{{cite arXiv|last=Hain|first=Richard|date=2014-03-25|title=Lectures on Moduli Spaces of Elliptic Curves|class=math.AG|eprint=0812.1803}}</ref> <sup>pg 10-11</sup> corresponding to elliptic curves with [[J-invariant|<math>j</math>-invariant]] equal to <math>1728</math> and <math>0</math> where the automorphism groups are of order 4, 6, respectively<ref>{{Cite book |last=Galbraith |first=Steven |chapter=Elliptic Curves |chapter-url=https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~sgal018/crypto-book/ch9.pdf |title=Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography |url=https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~sgal018/crypto-book/crypto-book.html |publisher=Cambridge University Press |via=The University of Auckland}}</ref> <sup>pg 170</sup>. One point in the [[Fundamental domain]] with stabilizer of order <math>4</math> corresponds to <math>\tau = i</math>, and the points corresponding to the stabilizer of order <math>6</math> correspond to <math>\tau = e^{2\pi i / 3}, e^{\pi i / 3}</math><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Serre, Jean-Pierre |title=A Course in Arithmetic |date=1973 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-1-4684-9884-4 |location=New York |oclc=853266550}}</ref><sup>pg 78</sup>.

==== Representing involutions of plane curves ====
Given a [[plane curve]] by its [[Weierstrass equation]]<math display="block">y^2 = x^3 + ax + b</math>and a solution <math>(t,s)</math>, generically for [[j-invariant]] <math>j \neq 0,1728</math>, there is the <math>\mathbb{Z}/2</math>-involution sending <math>(t,s)\mapsto (t,-s)</math>. In the special case of a curve with [[complex multiplication]]<math display="block"> y^2 = x^3 + ax</math>there the <math>\mathbb{Z}/4</math>-involution sending <math>(t,s)\mapsto (-t,\sqrt{-1}\cdot s)</math>. The other special case is when <math>a = 0</math>, so a curve of the form<math display="block">y^2 = x^3 + b</math> there is the <math>\mathbb{Z}/6</math>-involution sending <math>(t,s) \mapsto (\zeta_3 t,-s)</math> where <math>\zeta_3</math> is the third [[root of unity]] <math>e^{2\pi i / 3}</math>.

=== Fundamental domain and visualization ===
There is a subset of the upper-half plane called the [[Fundamental domain]] which contains every [[isomorphism class]] of elliptic curves. It is the subset<math display="block">D = \{z \in \mathfrak{h} : |z| \geq 1 \text{ and } \text{Re}(z) \leq 1/2 \}</math>It is useful to consider this space because it helps visualize the stack <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math>. From the quotient map<math display="block">\mathfrak{h} \to \text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\backslash \mathfrak{h}</math>the image of <math>D</math> is surjective and its interior is injective<ref name=":1" /><sup>pg 78</sup>. Also, the points on the boundary can be identified with their mirror image under the involution sending <math>\text{Re}(z) \mapsto -\text{Re}(z)</math>, so <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math> can be visualized as the projective curve <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> with a point removed at infinity<ref>{{Cite book |author=Henriques, André G |chapter=The Moduli stack of elliptic curves |url=https://www.math.ucla.edu/~mikehill/Research/surv-douglas2-201.pdf |title=Topological modular forms |editor=Douglas, Christopher L. |editor2=Francis, John |editor3=Henriques, André G |editor4=Hill, Michael A. |isbn=978-1-4704-1884-7|location=Providence, Rhode Island |oclc=884782304|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200609190825/https://www.math.ucla.edu/~mikehill/Research/surv-douglas2-201.pdf|archive-date=9 June 2020 |via=University of California, Los Angeles}}</ref><sup>pg 52</sup>.

=== Line bundles and modular functions ===
There are line bundles <math>\mathcal{L}^{\otimes k}</math> over the moduli stack <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math> whose sections correspond to [[Modular form|modular functions]] <math>f</math> on the upper-half plane <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>. On <math>\mathbb{C}\times\mathfrak{h}</math> there are <math>\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math>-actions compatible with the action on <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> given by<math display="block">\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \times {\displaystyle \mathbb {C} \times {\mathfrak {h}}} \to {\displaystyle \mathbb {C} \times {\mathfrak {h}}}</math>The degree <math>k</math> action is given by<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix} : (z,\tau ) \mapsto \left( (c\tau + d)^kz, \frac{a\tau + b}{c\tau + d} \right)</math>hence the trivial line bundle <math>\mathbb{C}\times\mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{h}</math> with the degree <math>k</math> action descends to a unique [[line bundle]] denoted <math>\mathcal{L}^{\otimes k}</math>. Notice the action on the factor <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is a [[Representation theory|representation]] of <math>\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math> on <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> hence such representations can be tensored together, showing <math>\mathcal{L}^{\otimes k} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes l} \cong \mathcal{L}^{\otimes (k + l)}</math>. The sections of <math>\mathcal{L}^{\otimes k}</math> are then functions  sections <math>f \in \Gamma(\mathbb{C}\times \mathfrak{h})</math> compatible with the action of <math>\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math>, or equivalently, functions <math>f:\mathfrak{h} \to \mathbb{C}</math> such that<math display="block"> f\left(
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d \end{pmatrix} \cdot \tau
\right) = (c\tau + d)^kf(\tau)</math> This is exactly the condition for a [[holomorphic function]] to be modular.

==== Modular forms ====
The modular forms are the modular functions which can be extended to the compactification<math display="block">\overline{\mathcal{L}^{\otimes k}} \to \overline{\mathcal{M}}_{1,1}</math>this is because in order to compactify the stack <math>\mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math>, a point at infinity must be added, which is done through a gluing process by gluing the <math>q</math>-disk (where a modular function has its <math>q</math>-expansion)<ref name=":2" /><sup>pgs 29-33</sup>.

=== Universal curves ===
Constructing the universal curves <math>\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{M}_{1,1}</math> is a two step process: (1) construct a versal curve <math>\mathcal{E}_{\mathfrak{h}} \to \mathfrak{h}</math> and then (2) show this behaves well with respect to the <math>\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math>-action on <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>. Combining these two actions together yields the quotient stack<math display="block">[(\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \ltimes \mathbb{Z}^2 )\backslash \mathbb{C}\times\mathfrak{h}]</math>

==== Versal curve ====
Every rank 2 <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-lattice in <math>\mathbb{C}</math> induces a canonical <math>\mathbb{Z}^{2}</math>-action on <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. As before, since every lattice is homothetic to a lattice of the form <math>(1,\tau)</math> then the action <math>(m,n)</math> sends a point <math>z \in \mathbb{C}</math> to<math display="block">(m ,n)\cdot z \mapsto z + m\cdot 1 + n\cdot\tau</math>Because the <math>\tau</math> in <math> \mathfrak{h}</math> can vary in this action, there is an induced <math>\mathbb{Z}^{2}</math>-action on <math>\mathbb{C}\times\mathfrak{h}</math><math display="block">(m ,n)\cdot (z, \tau) \mapsto (z + m\cdot 1 + n\cdot\tau, \tau)</math>giving the quotient space<math display="block">\mathcal{E}_\mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{h}</math>by projecting onto <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>.

==== SL<sub>2</sub>-action on Z<sup>2</sup> ====
There is a <math>\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math>-action on <math>\mathbb{Z}^{2}</math> which is compatible with the action on <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>, meaning given a point <math>z \in \mathfrak{h}</math> and a <math>g \in \text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math>, the new lattice <math>g\cdot z</math> and an induced action from <math>\mathbb{Z}^2 \cdot g</math>, which behaves as expected. This action is given by<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix} : (m, n) \mapsto (m,n)\cdot \begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}</math>which is [[matrix multiplication]] on the right, so<math display="block">(m,n)\cdot \begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix} = (
am + cn, bm + dn
)</math>
